concept.name: Tweezer bottom
concept.definition: A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose lows match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price floor, typically appearing in a downtrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same low as a minor bullish reversal signal, the mirror of the tweezer top, which gains weight when combined with other reversal shapes.
concept.intuition: The market probed the exact same floor twice and held both times, as if supported by tweezers at that price, suggesting buyers are defending that level.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: two or more candles (consecutive or separated) share essentially equal lows; the first is typically a black candle and the second a white candle in the classic downtrend form. The matching lows define an ad-hoc support level whose break invalidates the bullish reading.
concept.failure_modes: Matching lows are common by coincidence, so isolated tweezer bottoms carry little weight. In strong downtrends the double bottom at the lows often gives way to further declines.
concept.misconceptions: The candles need not be adjacent or similar in size; only the lows must match. It is a minor confirmation-level signal, not a major standalone reversal pattern.
concept.example: A stock falls and prints a black candle with a low of 22.00, then the next session dips to 22.00 again before closing higher as a white candle. The tweezer bottom marks 22.00 as support and hints at a possible bounce.
